what_its_for: Trastuzumab-dkst is a cancer medicine used to treat certain types of breast cancer and stomach cancer (gastric or gastroesophageal junction cancer) that have too much of a protein called HER2. It works by attaching to HER2 on cancer cells and helping your immune system slow down or stop cancer growth.
how_to_take: This medicine is given as an intravenous (IV) infusion, meaning it goes directly into your vein through a needle or catheter. A nurse or healthcare provider will give you this infusion at a clinic or hospital. Your first infusion is given slowly over about 90 minutes. If you tolerate it well, later infusions may be given over 30 minutes. You will be watched carefully during and after each infusion for any reactions.
dosing: Your doctor will determine your dose based on your body weight (in kilograms) and the type of cancer being treated. A common starting dose for breast cancer is 4 mg/kg, followed by 2 mg/kg weekly, or 8 mg/kg every 3 weeks followed by 6 mg/kg every 3 weeks. For stomach cancer, dosing is typically every 3 weeks. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions — never change your dose on your own.
missed_dose: Because this medicine is given by a healthcare provider, it is very important to keep all of your scheduled appointments. If you miss or need to reschedule an infusion, call your doctor or clinic right away. Do not wait until your next scheduled appointment — your treatment schedule may need to be adjusted.
storage: Trastuzumab-dkst is stored and prepared by healthcare professionals. The unopened vials should be kept in the refrigerator between 36°F and 46°F (2°C to 8°C). Do not freeze. Once mixed (reconstituted), the medicine should be kept in the refrigerator and used within 28 days. You do not need to store this medicine at home.
what_to_avoid: Tell your doctor about all medicines, vitamins, and supplements you take before starting treatment. Avoid becoming pregnant while on this medicine and for at least 7 months after your last dose, as it can harm an unborn baby. Do not breastfeed during treatment and for at least 7 months after your last infusion. Avoid live vaccines unless your doctor says it is safe. Talk to your doctor before having any surgery or dental procedures.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor or go to the emergency room right away if you experience: trouble breathing or shortness of breath, chest pain or tightness, rapid or irregular heartbeat, swelling of your ankles or legs, sudden weight gain (more than 5 pounds in a week), severe chills, fever, or shaking during or after your infusion, dizziness or feeling faint, severe nausea or vomiting, unusual bruising or bleeding, signs of infection (fever over 100.4°F, chills, cough), or any signs of a severe allergic reaction such as hives, rash, or swelling of the face or throat. Also let your doctor know if you feel more tired than usual or short of breath with everyday activities, as this medicine can affect your heart.
when_it_works: Most people do not feel this medicine working right away. It may take several weeks or months of treatment before your doctor can measure whether the cancer is responding. Your doctor will check your progress with regular tests, including imaging scans and blood tests. Do not stop treatment early just because you feel well — continue treatment as long as your doctor recommends.
special_populations: Pregnancy: Do not use this medicine if you are pregnant. It can cause serious harm or death to an unborn baby. Use effective birth control during treatment and for at least 7 months after your last dose. Tell your doctor right away if you become pregnant. Breastfeeding: Do not breastfeed during treatment or for at least 7 months after your last dose. Heart conditions: This medicine can weaken the heart. Tell your doctor if you have any heart problems before starting treatment. Your heart function will be checked with an echocardiogram or MUGA scan before and regularly during treatment. Elderly patients: Older adults may have a higher risk of heart problems with this medicine and should be monitored closely. Kidney or liver disease: Dose adjustments are not specifically required, but always inform your doctor of any organ problems.
